AssistantMessageToolRequest(name='create', tool_call_id='tooluse_yDkj9MwIq5F7kugNjXvwTi', arguments={'file_text': ' Cat FAQ

Everything you need to know

Frequently Asked
Cat Questions

Curious about your feline companion? We've got the answers.

Behaviour & Communication

Cats purr by rapidly dilating and constricting the glottis — the part of the larynx surrounding the vocal cords — as they breathe in and out. This produces a continuous rumbling sound at frequencies between 25 and 150 Hz.

While purring is most associated with contentment, cats also purr when anxious, injured, or unwell. Researchers believe the vibrations may even promote bone healing and reduce pain, making purring a self-soothing mechanism as much as a social signal.

A slow blink from a cat is a sign of trust and affection — often called a "cat kiss." In feline body language, closing the eyes around someone signals that you feel safe enough not to need your guard up.

You can return the gesture: make eye contact, then slowly close and open your eyes. Research by animal behaviourist Karen McComb found that cats are more likely to slow-blink back at humans who do this first.

This behaviour is rooted in instinct. In the wild, mother cats bring prey to their kittens to teach them hunting skills. When your cat brings you a "gift," it may be treating you as part of its family — sharing the spoils of the hunt with the pride.

Spayed or neutered cats still exhibit this behaviour because it's driven by deep predatory instincts rather than reproductive hormones. Keeping cats indoors or using a bell collar can help protect local wildlife.

Health & Care

Healthy adult cats (1–10 years) should see a vet at least once a year for a wellness exam, vaccinations, and parasite prevention. Kittens need more frequent visits — typically every 3–4 weeks until 16 weeks old — and senior cats (10+) benefit from check-ups every six months.

Don't wait for visible signs of illness; cats instinctively hide discomfort. Regular exams catch issues like dental disease, kidney problems, and hyperthyroidism early, when they're far easier to manage.

Most cats are fastidious self-groomers and rarely need bathing. However, a bath may be necessary if your cat:

  • Gets into something sticky, toxic, or foul-smelling
  • Has a skin condition requiring medicated shampoo
  • Is a show cat requiring a pristine coat
  • Has mobility issues that prevent self-grooming

When bathing is needed, use lukewarm water and a cat-specific shampoo — human shampoo can disrupt a cat's skin pH.

Increased thirst (polydipsia) is a symptom worth investigating. Common causes include:

  • Diabetes mellitus — insulin deficiency leading to high blood sugar
  • Chronic kidney disease — very common in older cats
  • Hyperthyroidism — overactive thyroid, especially in cats over 10
  • Urinary tract infection

If you notice a sustained change in your cat's water intake, book a vet visit promptly. A simple blood and urine panel can usually identify the cause.

Diet & Nutrition

No. Cats are obligate carnivores, meaning they require nutrients found only in animal tissue to survive. Key examples include:

  • Taurine — essential for heart function and vision; almost absent in plants
  • Arachidonic acid — a fatty acid cats cannot synthesise from plant precursors
  • Preformed vitamin A — cats cannot convert beta-carotene like humans can

A plant-based diet will lead to severe, potentially fatal deficiencies over time. Always feed cats a nutritionally complete food formulated for their life stage.

The classic image of a cat lapping up a saucer of milk is misleading. Most adult cats are lactose-intolerant: their digestive systems produce little to no lactase, the enzyme needed to break down milk sugar. Cow's milk can cause stomach upsets, diarrhoea, and gas.

If you want to give your cat a dairy treat, look for specially formulated "cat milk" with reduced lactose levels. But remember — it's still a treat, not a nutritional staple. Fresh water is always the best drink for a cat.

Always consult a qualified veterinarian for personalised advice about your cat.

Frequently Asked
Cat Questions

+

+ Curious about your feline companion? We've got the answers. +

+
+ +

+

Behaviour & Communication

+ +
+ +
+
+

Cats purr by rapidly dilating and constricting the glottis — the part of the larynx surrounding the vocal cords — as they breathe in and out. This produces a continuous rumbling sound at frequencies between 25 and 150 Hz.

+

While purring is most associated with contentment, cats also purr when anxious, injured, or unwell. Researchers believe the vibrations may even promote bone healing and reduce pain, making purring a self-soothing mechanism as much as a social signal.

+
+
+
+ +
+ +
+
+

A slow blink from a cat is a sign of trust and affection — often called a "cat kiss." In feline body language, closing the eyes around someone signals that you feel safe enough not to need your guard up.

+

You can return the gesture: make eye contact, then slowly close and open your eyes. Research by animal behaviourist Karen McComb found that cats are more likely to slow-blink back at humans who do this first.

+
+
+
+ +
+ +
+
+

This behaviour is rooted in instinct. In the wild, mother cats bring prey to their kittens to teach them hunting skills. When your cat brings you a "gift," it may be treating you as part of its family — sharing the spoils of the hunt with the pride.

+

Spayed or neutered cats still exhibit this behaviour because it's driven by deep predatory instincts rather than reproductive hormones. Keeping cats indoors or using a bell collar can help protect local wildlife.

+
+
+
+
+ + +
+

Health & Care

+ +
+ +
+
+

Healthy adult cats (1–10 years) should see a vet at least once a year for a wellness exam, vaccinations, and parasite prevention. Kittens need more frequent visits — typically every 3–4 weeks until 16 weeks old — and senior cats (10+) benefit from check-ups every six months.

+

Don't wait for visible signs of illness; cats instinctively hide discomfort. Regular exams catch issues like dental disease, kidney problems, and hyperthyroidism early, when they're far easier to manage.

+
+
+
+ +
+ +
+
+

Most cats are fastidious self-groomers and rarely need bathing. However, a bath may be necessary if your cat:

+
    +
  • Gets into something sticky, toxic, or foul-smelling
    • +
  • Has a skin condition requiring medicated shampoo
    • +
  • Is a show cat requiring a pristine coat
    • +
  • Has mobility issues that prevent self-grooming
    • +
+

When bathing is needed, use lukewarm water and a cat-specific shampoo — human shampoo can disrupt a cat's skin pH.

+
+
+
+ +
+ +
+
+

Increased thirst (polydipsia) is a symptom worth investigating. Common causes include:

+
    +
  • Diabetes mellitus — insulin deficiency leading to high blood sugar
    • +
  • Chronic kidney disease — very common in older cats
    • +
  • Hyperthyroidism — overactive thyroid, especially in cats over 10
    • +
  • Urinary tract infection
    • +
+

If you notice a sustained change in your cat's water intake, book a vet visit promptly. A simple blood and urine panel can usually identify the cause.

+
+
+
+
+ + +
+

Diet & Nutrition

+ +
+ +
+
+

No. Cats are obligate carnivores, meaning they require nutrients found only in animal tissue to survive. Key examples include:

+
    +
  • Taurine — essential for heart function and vision; almost absent in plants
    • +
  • Arachidonic acid — a fatty acid cats cannot synthesise from plant precursors
    • +
  • Preformed vitamin A — cats cannot convert beta-carotene like humans can
    • +
+

A plant-based diet will lead to severe, potentially fatal deficiencies over time. Always feed cats a nutritionally complete food formulated for their life stage.

+
+
+
+ +
+ +
+
+

The classic image of a cat lapping up a saucer of milk is misleading. Most adult cats are lactose-intolerant: their digestive systems produce little to no lactase, the enzyme needed to break down milk sugar. Cow's milk can cause stomach upsets, diarrhoea, and gas.

+

If you want to give your cat a dairy treat, look for specially formulated "cat milk" with reduced lactose levels. But remember — it's still a treat, not a nutritional staple. Fresh water is always the best drink for a cat.

+
+
+
+
+
+ +
+

Always consult a qualified veterinarian for personalised advice about your cat.
